headline: NASA diversifies contracts. Blue Origin resumes flights. Space Force invests.
deck: This week sees NASA expanding its reliance on SpaceX, while Blue Origin finally clears the air on New Glenn. Meanwhile, the Space Force is throwing cash at satellite networks.

stories.head: NASA adds missions to SpaceX crew contract
stories.body: NASA has decided to add more missions to its existing commercial crew contract with SpaceX, ensuring a backup plan if Boeing's CST-100 Starliner remains grounded. This move underscores NASA’s growing reliance on SpaceX, especially as Boeing’s spacecraft struggles with delays. The exact number of missions added hasn’t been disclosed, but it signals a clear preference for SpaceX’s operational reliability.
stories.soWhat: Boeing's woes are becoming SpaceX's gain, and it’s hard to see how Boeing can recover from this without a major overhaul.

stories.head: Blue Origin clears New Glenn launch failure investigation
stories.body: Blue Origin has completed its investigation into the New Glenn launch failure, allowing the rocket to resume preparations for future flights. The company is now hoping to avoid further detours, but the timeline for the next launch remains unclear. This comes after a series of setbacks that have kept New Glenn from its intended trajectory.
stories.soWhat: Resuming flights is one thing; actually launching successfully is another. Blue Origin still has a long road ahead to regain trust.

stories.head: Space Force awards $437M to Viasat and SES
stories.body: The Space Force has awarded a $437 million contract to Viasat and SES to develop a military satellite network involving four small satellites. This funding reflects a shift towards smaller, more agile satellite solutions in military applications, which could change the landscape of defense communications. The move is also a clear signal that the Space Force is prioritizing resilience over sheer size.
stories.soWhat: In an age of budget constraints, smaller satellites might just be the new black for military procurement.

watchlist.title: SpaceX's next Starship launch
watchlist.body: With the successful launch of Starship V3, keep an eye on how quickly SpaceX can iterate and address any remaining issues.

watchlist.title: True Anomaly's Series C impact
watchlist.body: True Anomaly's $190M raise could signal a shift in co-orbital security priorities, especially with DoD involvement.

watchlist.title: NASA's reorganization outcomes
watchlist.body: Watch for the effects of NASA's sweeping reorganization on project timelines and inter-agency collaboration.

watchlist.title: Blue Origin's next steps
watchlist.body: As Blue Origin prepares for its next launch, the industry will be watching closely to see if they can finally deliver.

talent.statLabel: Week-over-week growth in resumes from primes to Series B/C
talent.head: Talent is leaving big-aero — and it's not about money
talent.body: Compensation is not the gating factor. The complaint, almost universally, is schedule risk — the inability to ship anything quickly, the half-decade gap between joining and seeing flight hardware, the meeting that exists to schedule the meeting. The startups absorbing this talent will, in two years, be hard to compete with on a level playing field.

tickers.note: Virgin Galactic's stock remains stagnant as it awaits news on commercial flights, with investors growing impatient.
Lockheed Martin's stock is holding steady, but the company must adapt to the shifting dynamics of military satellite contracts.
Palantir's $480M extension on the TITAN program suggests its software remains critical for military operations.
Apple's interest in satellite technology could complicate the competitive landscape, as it eyes potential partnerships.
